reason: Corollas can be lanate (woolly), for example outside or in the throat. The examples are correct.
A spathe can be broad. Some examples describe the inner margin, not the whole spathe, but the pair itself is meaningful.
Spathe position (erect, spreading, connivent) is a real character. The specific position value would be better than the general attribute.
A corolla or its tube can be subglobose or urceolate, which is a spheroid shape.
Nuts can be tomentose.
A waxy bloom on a surface is a real presence character. 'Bloom' is epicuticular wax.
A staminal tube or column can be hairy or glabrous. The examples fit.
Floral discs are described as ovoid, hemispheric, cylindrical or spheroid. The general 3-D shape term fits, though a more specific shape term would be better where one exists.
Corollas can be viscid, often through glandular hairs.
The length of the spathe tube is measured in the examples.
Branches can persist or fall. 'Persistent to the trunk base' means they are not shed.
'Rugose when dry' is given without saying which organ. It may be the capsule wall or leaf, not the sporangium base. A rule would need the part named in the text.
Rosettes can be clumped, which is aggregated. The negated examples ('not clumped') are still the same character.
Cupules are pubescent on the inside or outside.
Nuts can have an acute or apiculate apex or base. The sharpness is of the nut tip, which is acceptable.
Leaf laminae can be lobed.
An epidermis can carry bristles, for example the adaxial leaf surface.
Stipules can be elongate (longer than wide).
An ovary can be pyramidal.
The gynostemium (orchid column) can be hairy, bearded or villous.
Sepals (and keels) can be firm in texture.
Involucres can be winged or wingless. Only one flora so far.
Lateral veins can form a reticulate pattern. A more specific reticulate term would be better, but the pair is meaningful.
Samaras can be pubescent, puberulent or glabrous.
'Spur' here is the nectar spur of a flower (orchid or similar), not a short shoot. The pair exists only through the wrong part.
Pinnules of ferns and compound leaves can be dissected.
An indusium can be leathery (coriaceous).
Glumes can be hispid.
The examples are the areole (scar) on a nutlet, not the cactus areole bud (PO_0025353). The part is the wrong one.
Epicalyx segments can be pilose, villous or glabrous.
Wood (secondary xylem) is described as dense.
Perianth lobes can be fleshy.
A lobe of a lamina can have a toothed margin. The statements say the margin is toothed, so the quality is carried by the lobe.
The length of a microsporophyll (cycad) is measured in the examples. Only one flora so far.
Labellum lobes or their apex or margin can be dentate.
Spathes can be spotted, for example in Araceae.
An endocarp can be subglobose.
A spadix appendix can be cylindrical.
Lemmas and their keels can be spinulose or spinose.
Stipules (or the stipule scar) can be annular. Part of the evidence is the scar, not the stipule, but the pair is meaningful.
Fern indusia can be J-shaped. Only one flora so far.
Leaf sheath auricles can be toothed or dentate.
'Apex asymmetrical' may describe the sheath apex or be a misread of the blade. Only one flora. A rule would need the text to name the sheath as the bearer.
Stelidia (orchid column arms) are described as subulate.
Vittae can be obscure or inconspicuous.
A labellum lobe margin can be entire.
'Spur' here is the flower nectar spur or its opening, not a short shoot. The pair exists only through the wrong part.
Legumes can have an acuminate apex.
Glumes have colours.
The examples are the areole (scar) on a nutlet or similar, not the cactus areole bud. The part is the wrong one.
Drupes can have an acute or apiculate apex.
Leaf scars can be present, prominent or conspicuous on branchlets.
'Divided into articles' means a jointed fruit (loment) that breaks into segments. It is not dissected (cut into lobes). A segmented or jointed term is needed.
Pinnules or segments can be cut or incised.
Style branches have colours.
'Arrondis' means rounded (round outline), not obtuse (apex angle). The PATO term is the wrong reading. A round-shape term is needed.
Scale leaves (cataphylls) can be triangular or deltoid.
A leaf apex can be hooked or falcate. 'Hooked' is a close fit to falciform.
Plant cells (mainly in mosses) can be pellucid (translucent).
The examples are about a hair-point, a separate structure on the apex. 'Present' belongs to the hair-point or awn, not to the leaf apex.
